name: Keynesian economics
scope: The body of macroeconomic ideas set out by John Maynard Keynes in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) and his other works, and the policy approach built on them: unemployment comes from insufficient aggregate demand, prices and wages adjust slowly, and government can stabilise the economy and promote full employment through fiscal and monetary policy (Britannica, Econlib, Investopedia). It covers Keynes's own writings and the Keynesian tradition as the defining sources describe it, including the post-war mainstream and the later new Keynesian refinements. It excludes monetarism, new classical economics and Austrian economics, which the sources present as rivals, and Keynes's views outside economics, such as probability theory or the Versailles settlement, except where his texts bear on the same questions.

summary: Keynesian economics is the body of macroeconomic ideas Keynes set out in the General Theory: unemployment results from insufficient aggregate demand, prices and wages adjust slowly, and government can stabilise output and employment through fiscal and monetary policy, including deficit spending in slumps. Keynes pursued this within capitalism, rejecting State Socialism and the gold standard while favouring lower interest for the rentier, redistribution and some socialisation of investment.
